Duele, duelen: “due” is one syllable: DWE-leh.
Garganta, gripe: a hard g, as in “get”.
No comas, no bebas, no salgas: the stress falls on the verb, and “no” is linked to it: “noCOmas”.
In Spanish you don’t say “mi cabeza” to talk about your own body: “Me duele LA cabeza” (my head hurts), not “me duele mi cabeza”. English uses “my”, Spanish uses “the”!

3. The negative imperative: NO + the “opposite” form + S
For “don’t do it!” with “tú”, take the polite form (usted) from chapter 22 and add -s. It’s the same “opposite” vowel:
For “usted”: you just add “no” in front: No hable. No coma. No salga.
The rule: -AR → -ES (no hables), -ER/-IR → -AS (no comas, no escribas). Always start from the “yo” form: salgo → no salgas, hago → no hagas.
4. Pronouns in the negative imperative: BEFORE
In the positive, the pronouns are attached at the end (dímelo). In the negative, they go BEFORE the verb, separately:

At the doctor’s: ¿Qué le pasa? (What’s the matter?) — ¿Desde cuándo? (Since when?) — Tome esto tres veces al día. (Take this three times a day.) — Le voy a hacer una receta. (I’ll write you a prescription.)

Diez consejos para una vida sana
A poster in the waiting room of the hospital where Mihai works.
One: eat five portions of fruit and vegetables a day. Don’t eat too much sugar.
Two: drink at least a litre and a half of water. Don’t drink lots of fizzy drinks.
Three: walk for thirty minutes a day. Use the stairs, not the lift.
Four: sleep between seven and eight hours. Don’t look at your phone in bed.
Five: don’t smoke. If you smoke, ask your doctor for help to quit.
Six: wash your hands often, especially before eating.
Seven: don’t sit down all day. Get up every hour.
Eight: laugh a lot and spend time with friends and family.
Nine: don’t take medicines without asking your doctor or pharmacist.
Ten: see your doctor once a year, even if nothing hurts.
And remember: health is the most important thing!

Mihai is always giving advice to his patients: sleep more, eat better, don’t smoke, do some exercise.
But he doesn’t follow his own advice. He works too much, sleeps little and eats sandwiches at all hours.
One morning he woke up with a terrible backache. He couldn’t move.
Ana looked at him from the doorway and said: “You’re not going to work today. Today you’re going to the doctor.”
“Ana, I am a doctor,” he protested. “That’s exactly why,” she answered.
At the health centre, Dr Ruiz examined him carefully. She asked him lots of questions.
“How many hours do you sleep?” “About five.” “Do you exercise?” “Well… I take the stairs at the hospital.”
“And stress?” Mihai laughed. “I work in A&E, doctor.”
The doctor took off her glasses and looked at him very seriously.
“Dr Popescu, you know perfectly well what I’m going to tell you. But I’m going to tell you anyway.”
“Rest for three days. Don’t lift anything heavy. Take these pills for the pain, but only after meals.”
“And most importantly: don’t do more than four night shifts a month. If you carry on like this, the next patient will be you.”
Mihai left the health centre deep in thought. The doctor was right: he had been tired for months.
That evening he made a list of changes and stuck it on the fridge:
“Sleep seven hours. Walk thirty minutes a day. Cook with Ana on Sundays. Don’t look at my phone in bed.”
Ana read the list and added one more line in red pen: “And listen to your girlfriend. She’s always right.”
Three weeks later, Mihai’s back no longer hurt. He was sleeping better, he was in a better mood and he had lost three kilos.
One day a patient asked him: “Doctor, do you follow your own advice?”. Mihai smiled: “Now I do.”
Ana, of course, said nothing. She just smiled and served him a salad.
